results.title: Quantitative Methods In The Social Sciences
results.content: Quantitative Methods In The Social Sciences - MISTT Innovation Hub Home_/_Columbia_/_ Quantitative Methods In The Social Sciences Quantitative Methods In The Social Sciences Quantitative Methods In The Social Sciences In the realm of social sciences, researchers often face the challenge of studying complex human behaviors, attitudes, and social phenomena. * Key Characteristics of Quantitative Methods * What are some common quantitative research designs in the social sciences? Quantitative methods in the social sciences are research techniques that rely on numerical data and statistical analysis. ### Key Characteristics of Quantitative Methods Quantitative methods possess several distinctive characteristics that set them apart from other research approaches: * **Empirical Focus:** Quantitative methods prioritize empirical data, emphasizing the collection of measurable observations or facts. * **Objective Approach:** These methods aim to minimize researcher bias by employing standardized data collection and analysis techniques. * **Statistical Analysis:** Quantitative research heavily relies on statistical tools to interpret and draw meaningful conclusions from the data. Quantitative methods find extensive applications across various social science disciplines, offering valuable insights and informing policy decisions. In sociology, quantitative methods are used to study a wide range of social issues and phenomena. Quantitative methods play a crucial role in political science, helping researchers analyze voting patterns, understand public opinion, and evaluate the impact of policies. Quantitative methods offer several advantages in social science research. 💡 It is crucial for social scientists to carefully consider the strengths and limitations of quantitative methods and employ a mixed-methods approach when appropriate, combining quantitative and qualitative techniques to gain a comprehensive understanding of social phenomena. As technology advances and data collection becomes more accessible, quantitative methods in the social sciences are likely to evolve and expand their scope. Quantitative methods in the social sciences serve as a vital tool for researchers to study and understand complex human behaviors and social structures. While quantitative methods have their limitations, their strengths and potential for integration with qualitative approaches make them an indispensable part of the social science research toolkit. Statistical analysis is crucial in quantitative methods as it allows researchers to make sense of the collected data.

results.title: The importance of qualitative social research for effective fisheries management
results.content: Until recently, fisheries managers and researchers have struggled to develop effective methods and data for social and economic analysis that can integrate with the predominantly biological approaches to fisheries management. This paper uses three divergent case studies to demonstrate the value of using qualitative social science approaches to complement more conventional quantitative methods to improve the knowledge base for fisheries management. The study aimed at evaluating how fishers could provide consistent and reliable data on major fish species/groups comparable with official catch data and to explore the potential of increasing their participation in fishery management. The Community-Based Resource Enhancement (CBRE) process, implemented continuously from 2006 to 2019, include social and biophysical preparation, formulation of fisheries management and governance strategies, release of hatchery-reared juveniles, monitoring and periodic assessment, and socioeconomic impact assessment. It has been proposed that local and national management policies and practices can be more effective if they are more gender equitable and better consider the differences in how men and women participate in natural resource use and in the community, taking into account their potentially different goals.3 The CGIAR Research Program on Aquatic Agricultural Systems (AAS), led by WorldFish, aims to deliver increased food security and income for the millions of people living in and depending on aquatic agricultural systems, and intends to take a gender-transformative approach to integrating gender into research in development. The components include the need to: (1) prioritize and select target species for enhancement; (2) develop a species management plan that identifies harvest opportunity, stock rebuilding goals, and genetic objectives; (3) define quantitative measures of success; (4) use genetic resource management to avoid deleterious genetic effects; (5) use disease and health management; (6) consider ecological, biological, and life-history patterns when forming enhancement objectives and tactics; (7) identify released hatchery fish and assess stocking impacts; (8) use an empirical process for defining optimum release strategies; (9) identify economic and policy guidelines; and (10) use adaptive management. To examine the importance of gender to the understanding of marine ecology, we identified 106 case studies of small-scale fisheries from the last 20 years that detail the participation of women in fishing (data on women fishers being the most common limiting factor to gender analysis).

Title: On Think Tanks | Impact of social sciences: maximizing the impact of academic research
A monthly round up of the latest content and activities from OTT and our global community. # Impact of Social Sciences: Maximizing the impact of academic research. The London School of Economics has a great project and blog on the Impact of Social Sciences (Maximizing the impact of academic research, is the sub-title). The Impact of Social Sciences aims to:. [D]emonstrate how academic research in the social sciences achieves public policy impacts, contributes to economic prosperity and informs public understanding of policy issues and economic and social changes. In order to achieve this is will seek to:. [D]evelop precise methods for measuring and evaluating the impact of research in the public sphere. We have begun to develop quantitative metrics for measuring impact  and have performed comparative analyses based on a pilot study of 120 academics pulled from a variety of social science disciplines. The programme is co-ordinated by a central team in the London School of Economics Public Policy Group and involves the Grantham Institute for Climate Change at Imperial College London, the Sustainability Research Institute at Leeds University, LSE Health and the LSE Centre for Economic Performance. They have already put together some very interesting products and services:. It provides a large menu of sound and evidence-based advice and guidance on how to ensure that your work achieves its maximum visibility and influence with both academic and external audiences. ## Related content. ## Reflecting on the On Think Tanks School for Thinktankers: Working with diaspora think tanks. ## Strengthening Myanmar’s knowledge infrastructure: Why diaspora think tanks matter. ## Ten years of the Open Think Tank Directory: From a spreadsheet to a shared public resource. ## Advancing resilience and transformation in policy ecosystems. ## “It wasn’t just research”: How CHRICED helped turn Kano’s maternal health crisis into a law. ## Education won’t scale from within the education sector alone. ## What we heard in Nairobi: 2025 State of the Sector report launch. ## Think tank state of the sector survey 2026.

results.title: Social sustainability in Bangladesh marine fisheries management: A case ...
results.content: Social sustainability in Bangladesh marine fisheries management: A case from Hatiya fishing community - ScienceDirect. Social sustainability in Bangladesh marine fisheries management: A case from Hatiya fishing community. This study assesses the social sustainability in Bangladesh marine fisheries management gaining insights from the coastal and marine fisheries-dependent communities of Hatiya Upazila in 2021–2022 using a mixed method approach especially focusing on the social issues during the marine fishing ban. Finally, this study provides some way forward to bring social sustainability that is affected due to the marine fishing ban as well as to partly meet the targets of Sustainable Development Goals 1, 2, 14 and 15. However, scarce studies are available on the social impact of the 65-day marine fishing ban on the fishery-dependent communities of coastal Bangladesh such as Islam et al. As such, the overall objective of this study is to assess the impacts of the marine fishing ban on the social aspects of sustainability of the fishery-reliant peoples in Bangladesh and suggest ways for improvement. Security of the daily basic needs of fishers' families during the fishing ban must be ensured in order to achieve social sustainability. Though the 65-day marine fishing ban has shown an affirmative impact on fish production, the socio-economic conditions of the fishers and their household members have been adversely affected leading to poor social sustainability. * e.**Financial support for fishers' households during the ban:** The government should consider providing financial assistance to fishers during the fishing ban to promote social sustainability in fisheries management, as all of the fishers stated that they have to buy other daily goods like groceries and children's education and healthcare. So, insurance coverage due to the impacts of the fishing ban might bring social sustainability for the poor fishers of Bangladesh. Moreover, this study used a mixed-method approach (both qualitative and quantitative methods) for assessing the social sustainability of the local fishers, but social sustainability indicators based mixed-method approach might provide a more robust outcome of the impacts of the marine fishing ban.
